content_voiceover: This diagram shows how red cells are destroyed in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and it's important to understand the two mechanisms because they guide treatment. IgG or IgM antibodies bind to red cell antigens, and this can trigger complement activation. If complement activation goes all the way to the membrane attack complex, you get complement-mediated lysis directly in the bloodstream — that's intravascular hemolysis. This is managed acutely by keeping the patient warm, especially relevant in cold agglutinin disease, and plasmapheresis in severe cases. More commonly, though, red cells coated with IgG or with complement fragments like C3b are recognized by macrophages in the reticuloendothelial system — this is extravascular hemolysis. Cells coated with complement are cleared mainly in the liver via complement receptors, while IgG-coated cells are cleared mainly in the spleen via Fc-gamma receptors. Because extravascular hemolysis is the dominant pathway in most AIHA, treatment targets this axis first: corticosteroids like prednisone, IVIG to block Fc-gamma receptors, and splenectomy for refractory cases. For antibody production itself, second-line therapy includes rituximab, an anti-CD20 antibody, plus azathioprine or cyclophosphamide as immunosuppressants.
keypoints: Intravascular hemolysis: complement-mediated lysis directly in the bloodstream — treat with warming the patient and plasmapheresis.
Extravascular hemolysis: IgG-coated RBCs cleared by the spleen via Fc-gamma receptors; complement-coated RBCs cleared by the liver via complement receptors.
First-line treatment targets extravascular hemolysis: prednisone, IVIG, and splenectomy.
Second-line therapy reduces antibody production: rituximab (anti-CD20), azathioprine, cyclophosphamide.
keypoint_voiceover: Know your two hemolysis pathways. Intravascular hemolysis is complement-mediated lysis directly in the blood, managed with warming the patient and plasmapheresis. Extravascular hemolysis is more common — IgG-coated cells get cleared in the spleen via Fc-gamma receptors, while complement-coated cells get cleared in the liver via complement receptors. First-line treatment for extravascular hemolysis is prednisone, IVIG, and splenectomy. Second-line therapy aimed at reducing antibody production includes rituximab, azathioprine, and cyclophosphamide.
